title: Guards Audit
eyebrow: Audit for approval · GitHub issue 285, "Guards block only unrecoverable actions" · nothing changed yet

short.lead: I went through every hook in hook.py (a hook is an automatic check) that can stop me. My test was yours: only data loss with no way back, or a change to someone else's work, should stop me. Nine kinds of destructive action are refused outright, and each refusal names the safe way to do the job instead. Deletes are refused only when the data isn't saved. You are asked only when no safe way exists and I cite a source proving it. Four refusals become reminders. The background-work guard is removed entirely. Publishing a page is never refused again.
short.hint: Tap a card for what it guards today and what changes.
key: Refused, with the safe way named
items: Three things no guard may ever stop

You set these three requirements at 14:45 on 15 October. First, a routine commit or push to an agent-created branch other than main is never blocked. That means a branch named AjsAgent/ or claude/, or a helper's own working-copy branch. Second, publishing an artifact is never blocked. Third, the agent, or a helper it starts, can always change its own files inside the folder it was given. No prompt, refusal or timeout applies to any of them.
Nothing from you. It will be built first and tested by verify.py.
Nine kinds of destructive action, refused outright

1. Pushing or committing to main (the shared primary branch): open a pull request instead. 2. Commits, merges, rebases, cherry-picks and reverts on a branch the guard can't confirm is mine: make a new AjsAgent/ branch and commit there. 3. A force-push (overwriting history on the server), or a push with --all or --mirror: push a new branch instead. 4. Deleting a branch, local (branch -D) or remote (push --delete): leave it for you to delete. 5. git clean (deletes untracked files): move them into a _to_delete/ folder. 6. filter-branch (rewrites all history): rewrite on a copy branch. 7. git reset, git checkout -- or git restore while uncommitted work (changes not yet saved in git) exists: commit it on a new branch first. 8. stash drop or clear (discarding set-aside work): keep the stash. 9. Truncating (emptying) a file: write a new file beside it.
Nothing from you. You are asked only when no safe way exists and I cite a source proving it, such as the git manual.
Deletes are refused only when the file isn't saved

Today every delete command (rm) asks you first, even for a committed file git can restore. After this, a delete is refused in two cases. One is a recursive delete, which removes a whole folder (rm -r, rmdir /s, Remove-Item -Recurse). The other is a delete of a file that has uncommitted changes or was never committed. The refusal says to move the files into a _to_delete/ folder instead. Deleting a committed, unchanged file goes through, because git can bring it back.
Background work and process kills stop asking

These stop asking: background or hidden commands (nohup, a trailing &, Start-Process, background jobs), cutting a wait's output short with tail or head, and killing a process. None of these changes a branch or deletes saved work. The "Never hide work" rule text goes too, along with its 5-minute stall-check reminder.

The first three are refused today and become reminders. First, publishing a page not built by make_page.py. Second, a Claude credit line or a claude/ branch name on GitHub, and an issue without its sections. Third, a third helper (a sub-agent) running, or a helper starting its own helper. Fourth, overwriting a whole file. Today it always asks you first. Afterwards it goes through, unless the file has uncommitted changes. In that case it is refused, and the refusal says to commit first.

Today one unanswered prompt (a question asking for your OK) makes every later prompt in the session get refused straight away. That chain of refusals blocked both page publishes and the commit of the automatic-pages page. After this, you are asked only in the rare case where no safe way exists and I have cited a source proving it. The timer applies only to those prompts, never to anything else, such as publishing a page. Each prompt waits on its own, and nothing is refused because an earlier prompt went unanswered.

The design-loop lock stops code edits until you approve a build plan. You chose to keep it blocking (15 October, 15:04). So every plan reaches you as a page first, even though the helpers that write the code must wait while you're away.
Nothing more; your pick is recorded.

choices: What should the design-loop lock do?
Code edits go through, with a reminder that the plan hasn't been approved. It matches your test, but nothing forces plans to reach you as a page first.
Plans always reach you first, but builders stall while you're away.
It doesn't protect data, so your test says reminder; the cost is that sending the plan as a page first becomes a habit rather than an enforced rule.
